To investigate the substitution sites of Cr into Co O , the X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) characterizations at Co K-edge were carried out. As shown in Figure R2, the FT-EXAFS spectrum of Cr-Co O at Co K-edge is almost identical to that of Co O , except the decreased intensity of Co -Co (tetrahedral site), which indicates the Cr elements occupy the Co position in the lattice of Cr-Co O .
Besides, Raman spectroscopy can probe the vibrational modes of a crystal lattice, which are associated with specific atomic bond vibrations. Consequently, the positions of Raman peaks can be directly correlated with different coordination environments. The Co O spinel presents distinctive Raman modes, including E , F , and A modes, as demonstrated in Figure R3. Specially, the F mode (524 cm-1) is in connection with the stretching of CoO (Co -O), while the A mode (692 cm-1) and E mode (484 cm-1) are in connection with the stretching of CoO (Co -O) (J. Am. Chem. Soc., 2021, 143, 5201-5211; J. Am. Chem. Soc., 2023, 145, 17995-18006; Phys. Status Solidi (b), 2016, 253, 2270-2282; Nat. Commun., 2021, 12, 3036). Compared with Co O , the A mode and E mode in the Cr-Co O catalyst remain unchanged, while the F mode shifts. This further confirms that Cr substitutes for the Co position in the Co O lattice.

This indicates the structure of Cr in the Co position of Co O lattice possesses much lower energy, suggesting the Cr elements preferentially occupy the Co position in the lattice of Co O .

Response: Thanks for the reviewer’s valuable comment. Currently, among non-precious metal-based catalysts, only cobalt- and manganese-based systems have demonstrated practical capability for the acidic OER in PEMWE. In this context, Co O -based electrocatalysts have shown promising activity for the OER in acidic electrolytes and have thus garnered considerable recent attention. However, the widespread application of Co O is hampered by its limited stability due to the inevitable dissolution of cobalt ions under acidic conditions. More critically, Co O undergoes significant surface reconstruction during OER, leading to the formation of soluble and deactivated high-valence Co4+ species. This process is a primary cause of structural collapse. Therefore, stabilizing the lattice and electronic structures of Co O presents a promising strategy for enhancing its acidic OER performance.
In this manuscript, we have fabricated Cr-Co O catalyst with the formation of Cr -O-Co coordination environment and Cr3+-OH species modification on surface. It is crucial to note that the active sites in Cr-Co O remain centered on Co, given that Cr O itself is inactive toward the acidic OER, as corroborated by Figure R12. In addition, the characteristic binding energies for Cr3+ and Cr6+ species are assigned to approximately 576 eV and 580 eV, respectively. The in situ XPS spectra of the Cr 2p core level in Cr-Co O show no discernible signal at 580 eV, ruling out the over-oxidation of Cr3+ to Cr6+ under operating conditions (Figure R13).

Comment 8: The authors consistently argue that the enhancement in water dissociation in catalyst-electrolyte interface are originated from OH* on Cr site. However, the DFT calculation presented for Cr-Co O model without OH* already show a decrease in the Gibbs free energy for the H O dissociation step. To substantiate the claim thar Cr-OH* is the origin of the enhancement of water dissociation, please include DFT calculations that explicitly incorporate pre-adsorbed OH* on Cr, and compare the full reaction profiles with vs without OH*.
Response: Thanks for the reviewer’s valuable comment. We apologize for our unclear statements, which may have caused a misunderstanding for the reviewer. The DFT calculations presented in this manuscript were performed on the models of Cr-Co O with OH* adsorbed on the Cr site (denoted as Cr-Co O ) and Co O , respectively. To substantiate the claim thar Cr-OH* is the origin of the enhancement of water dissociation, we have provided the DFT calculations on the model of Cr-Co O without the OH* adsorbed on the Cr site (Cr -Co O ) (Figure R15). As shown in Figure R16, the water dissociation energy of Cr-Co O with the OH* adsorbed on the Cr site is much lower than that of Cr-Co O without the OH* adsorbed on the Cr site, suggesting the introduction of Cr-OH* can be favorable for the water dissociation process.
Figure R15. (a) and (b) are the top view and side view of Co O (311) surface with Cr atom substitutes the Co site (Cr -Co O ). The blue balls, grey ball, and red balls represent Co atoms, Cr atom, and O atoms, respectively.
Figure R16. DFT calculated the energy barrier of water dissociation for Cr-Co O with OH* pre-adsorbed on the Cr site (denoted as Cr-Co O ) and Cr-Co O without OH* pre-adsorbed on the Cr site (denoted as P-Cr-Co O ).
Accordingly, the Figures R15 and R16 have been added in the Revised Supporting Information as Figures S35 and S39. The related information has been updated in the Revised Manuscript as follow:
“The calculated model of Co O was shown in Figure S34. The different substitution sites of Cr into Co O were considered. As shown in Figures S35 and S36, the calculated formation energy of Cr -Co O and Cr -Co O is -2.00 eV and -1.12 eV, respectively. This indicates the structure of Cr in the Co position of Co O lattice possesses much lower energy, suggesting the Cr elements preferentially occupy the Co position in the lattice of Co O , in good agreement with the previous analysis. In conjunction with the fact that Cr3+-OH surface species exists under realistic catalytic conditions, the structure depicted in Figure S37 was chosen for modeling the Cr-Co O catalyst with OH* pre-adsorbed on the Cr site (denoted as Cr-Co O ).” (Page 12 in the revised manuscript)
